newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress, White House near deal on U.N. dues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress, White House near deal on U.N. dues.

text.p: Members of Congress and administration officials thrashed out final details on Wednesday of a bill that would pay off most of Washington's massive arrears to the United Nations.

The Senate Foreign Relations Committee said its top Republicans and Democrats had reached a provisional deal under which the United States would pay the world body $819 million over three years in back dues.

As a condition of the payment, according to the office of committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, the bill would demand a string of U.N. spending cuts, a reduction in U.S. annual dues and other concessions.

Committee spokesman Marc Thiessen said it was "pretty much a done deal" and forecast that the measure would be approved on Thursday by the committee and passed by the full Senate before the July 4 (Independence Day) national holiday.
But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said while Secretary of State Madeleine Albright welcomed the "progress" that had been made the accord had not yet been finalised.
"We still do need to do a lot more work to complete a deal," Burns said, adding that the total amount of money to be paid "is one of the issues that requires further work."
"The key will be in completing an agreement and working out the final details and that is happening as we speak," he told a news briefing.

U.S. debts to the United Nations have been a running sore for years, with Washington accused even by its closest allies of being a "deadbeat," but conservative Republicans refused to pay an extra cent to what they call a spendthrift bureaucracy.

Administration officials have insisted to Congress that it must pay the debt if U.S. credibility at the United Nations is to be preserved. The United Nations said the United States owes it more than $1 billion, but the deal hammered out by Helms and Democratic Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware said $819 million is the upper limit.
The Washington Post reported on Wednesday the bill would also "forgive" $106 million Washington says it is owed by the United Nations. The world body disputes that it owes that sum.

In New York, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard gave a "so far, so good" response, saying Secretary-General Kofi Annan was "encouraged" by the reports. He would not comment on the difference between the $819 million being discussed in Congress and what the United Nations claims is owed.

A key condition for the payment would be U.N. agreement to reduce the U.S. share of its regular budget from the current 25 percent to 22 percent in the second year of the deal and 20 percent in the third year. The U.S. share of the peacekeeping budget would be cut from 31 to 25 percent.

Other conditions for the United States to pay its dues for 1998-99 would require a negative growth U.N. budget, a $900 million cap on U.S. payments to international organisations and repayment for U.S. aid to U.N. peacekeeping operations.

Other conditions included a ban on global U.N. conferences in cities other than New York, Geneva, Rome and Vienna and a cut in foreign aid to nations whose U.N. diplomats owe unpaid parking fines by 110 percent of the amount of the fines.
The State Department says Russia is the leading parking violator.

The bill would also merge the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and the United States Information Agency into the State Department, in line with President Bill Clinton's proposal, as well as giving the State Department more control over the Agency for International Development.

Sen. Richard Luger of Indiana, one of the most respected Republicans on the Foreign Relations Committee, said the payment schedule should be changed to two years, the period over which this Congress has jurisdiction, rather than three.

Lugar said the Helms-Biden deal could leave allies such as France, Britain and the Netherlands holding the bag for the U.S. part of multilateral peacekeeping debt if the demanded U.N. reforms were never carried out.
